source: Wiley (1998) Expertise as mental set: the effects of domain knowledge in creative problem solving
finding: Domain knowledge acts as a mental set outside chess. People who knew more baseball solved fewer remote-associates items when the baseball answer was wrong. People who knew less baseball were not hurt.
numbers: Exp 1, N=24 (median split on baseball knowledge, 12 per group). Proportion correct, high knowledge: neutral .50, consistent .38, misleading .15. Low knowledge: neutral .50, consistent .40, misleading .40. Knowledge x trial type F(2,44)=4.06, p<.02. Baseball intrusions on misleading items .31 (high) vs .11 (low), p<.10. Response time on misleading items 31.4 s (high) vs 23.0 s (low).
limits: Median split, so the 'high' group was only intermediate knowledge (b03 checks the top scorers). Word-association task, not a move-choice task. Small N.
agent_relevance: Strong prior knowledge can lower accuracy exactly where the primed answer is wrong. An agent with rich domain priors needs a check that the primed answer is not the only one tried.

source: Wiley (1998) Expertise as mental set: the effects of domain knowledge in creative problem solving
finding: A plain warning not to use the domain knowledge did not remove the fixation in high-knowledge people. It may have made low-knowledge people more fixated on all items.
numbers: Exp 2, N=20 (5 subjects per knowledge x warning cell). Without warning, high-knowledge: misleading .20 vs neutral .58. With warning: misleading .30 vs neutral .52. Warning did not shrink the misleading effect for high knowledge: F(1,16)=1.89, p>.10. Without warning the effect replicated: F(1,8)=8.34, p<.02.
limits: Tiny cells (5 subjects). The warning was one sentence given at practice. Null result with low power.
agent_relevance: Telling a model 'do not use the obvious method' may not be enough on its own. Compare the partial effect of Luchins' 'Don't be blind' instruction in the A10.01 file.

source: Wiley (1998) Expertise as mental set: the effects of domain knowledge in creative problem solving
finding: Across the three experiments the misleading cost was reliably larger for high-knowledge subjects, and the top-knowledge subset showed it too. In Exp 3, delay before retest helped low-knowledge people and did not help high-knowledge people.
numbers: Pooled Exp 1-3 (N=54): knowledge x trial type for correct solutions F(1,52)=17.66, p<.0001; response time F(1,52)=8.15, p<.01; intrusions t(52)=2.25, p<.03. Top 10 knowledge subjects: misleading items solved far less than neutral, F(1,9)=62.02, p<.0001; intrusions .30 of misleading items; time 30.5 s vs 20.7 s (F(1,9)=10.30, p<.01). Exp 3: low-knowledge subjects solved more at retest after a delay (positive incubation); high-knowledge subjects solved more at an immediate retest (negative incubation).
limits: Incubation result comes from small cells in Exp 3. One task type (RAT with baseball primes).
agent_relevance: Waiting does not fix a block that comes from the solver's own strong knowledge. An outside change of view is needed, not more time.

source: Wiley (1998) Expertise as mental set: the effects of domain knowledge in creative problem solving
finding: Wiley's conditions for the effect: a productive (creative) task, and a task hard enough that low-knowledge people still engage with it. Low-knowledge, not zero-knowledge, people were the flexible ones. The misleading effect replicated in three separate samples.
numbers: Misleading effect for high-knowledge subjects found in Exp 1, in the no-warning cell of Exp 2, and in the no-fixation cell of Exp 3. Response-time effect significant in Exp 2, near significance in Exp 3, not in Exp 1. The intrusion effect was not significant in any single experiment.
quote: domain knowledge can indeed act as a mental set
limits: Author's own interpretation. Intrusion and time effects were less consistent than the accuracy effect.
agent_relevance: Expect the block when the correct answer lies outside the primed region of an open-ended task. In routine tasks, priors help.

source: Wiley (1998) Expertise as mental set: the effects of domain knowledge in creative problem solving
finding: Knowledge groups were weak compared with earlier baseball-expert studies, which Wiley flags as a concern: the effect may be an intermediate-knowledge effect.
numbers: Questionnaire of 45 items; low group below 15, high group 15 or more. Ten highest scorers across non-manipulated cells averaged 32.3, versus 41.3 and 40.0 in the Voss et al. (1980) high-knowledge groups.
limits: This is a limit on the claim, not on the data. True masters were not tested here (chess masters were tested by Bilalic et al.; see A10.01).
agent_relevance: Do not read this as proof that the top expert is blocked most. For that, see the chess studies.

source: Ninomiya, Terai and Miwa (2022) Differences in the distribution of attention to trained procedure between finders and non-finders of the alternative better procedure
finding: Computerised water-jar task with 50 critical trials: most people eventually drop the trained route, but a third do not within the session. The set weakens with repeated experience.
numbers: 60 Nagoya undergraduates, 90 min. 3 induction + 5 set + 50 critical (trials 9-58) + 2 test trials. 46 analysed (1 quit, 4 unclear reports, 9 found the alternative on the very first critical trial). 67% (31 of 46) found the shorter route before the last critical trial. Eye-tracked subgroup: 21 finders, 15 non-finders; finders found it on average at trial 17.85.
limits: Japanese undergraduates, one task. The 9 who escaped on trial 9 were removed, which removes the weakest sets.
agent_relevance: Einstellung is a delay more than a permanent lock over a long run of problems. Count trials to switch, not only whether the switch happens.

source: Ninomiya, Terai and Miwa (2022) Differences in the distribution of attention to trained procedure between finders and non-finders of the alternative better procedure
finding: People who later found the better route already looked more at information not tied to the trained procedure while the trained procedure still worked. The difference was absent at the start and grew with repetition.
numbers: First set trial: no group difference (gaze centre 97.85 vs 99.09 px; left-area fixation 14.0% vs 16.3%). Two trials before discovery: gaze centre 112.3 vs 178.8 px, F(1,34)=6.22, p=.018, eta2G=.15; left-area dwell 11.1% vs 3.1%, F(1,34)=5.18, p=.029. At the discovery trial: gaze centre F(1,34)=87.16, eta2G=.72.
quote: pay a certain amount of attention to information unrelated to the familiar procedure even when the familiar procedure is functioning well
limits: Correlational (finder status is defined after the fact). 21 vs 15 players. Gaze is a proxy for attention.
agent_relevance: Suggests keeping some attention on off-route information even when the known route works. For an agent: keep a small budget for checking alternatives while the current method still succeeds.

source: DeCaro (2016) Inducing mental set constrains procedural flexibility and conceptual understanding in mathematics
finding: Order of practice problems sets the mental set in maths. Doing multi-step problems first made adults use the shortcut less on later shortcut-friendly problems, while accuracy stayed equal.
numbers: Exp 1, N=41 undergraduates. Set-problem accuracy 97.7% (shortcut-first) vs 98.8% (complex-first), p=.306. Shortcut used on 56% (shortcut-first) vs 19% (complex-first), chi2(1,N=34)=4.86, p=.028 (7 excluded for uncodable work).
limits: Maths equivalence problems, not chess. Strategies were hand-coded and 7 of 41 were excluded. Accuracy is equal, so the cost is only in efficiency.
agent_relevance: Equal accuracy hides the cost. Log route cost, not only correctness, when judging whether a method has hardened.

source: DeCaro (2016) Inducing mental set constrains procedural flexibility and conceptual understanding in mathematics
finding: The set carried over to a later test: lower conceptual understanding and fewer different correct strategies, but no loss in procedure accuracy or transfer.
numbers: Exp 1 posttest, complex-first vs shortcut-first: conceptual knowledge F(1,39)=4.67, p=.037, partial eta2=.11. Procedural knowledge F<1; transfer F(1,39)=2.50, p=.122; flexibility knowledge F<1. Number of different correct strategies F(1,33)=4.91, p=.034, partial eta2=.13; grouping strategy use 39.9% vs 20.4%, d=.56.
limits: Posttest p values sit near .03 to .04 in cells of about 20. One lab.
agent_relevance: Practice order may shape what is understood, not only what is done. Order of lessons in context may matter.

source: DeCaro (2016) Inducing mental set constrains procedural flexibility and conceptual understanding in mathematics
finding: Replicated in 5th and 6th graders: complex-first order gave less shortcut use, lower conceptual and flexibility knowledge, and less flexible use at test. The test effect was smaller than in adults.
numbers: Exp 2, N=87 children (shortcut analysis N=66 after exclusions as reported). Shortcut use 10% (complex-first) vs 30% (shortcut-first), chi2(1,N=66)=5.21, p=.022. Set-problem accuracy 96.5% vs 97.0%. Conceptual knowledge F(1,82)=5.13, p=.026, partial eta2=.06; flexibility knowledge F(1,82)=6.54, p=.012, partial eta2=.07; flexible use F(1,76)=5.29, p=.024. Grouping strategy at test 12.0% vs 23.0%, d=.35.
limits: Smaller effect at test (d=.35 vs .56 in adults). Shortcut use was low in both groups.
agent_relevance: Same sign across age. Effect sizes are small to medium.

source: Fang et al. (2026) Semantic accessibility is associated with reduced experience-induced heuristic fixation in creative problem solving
finding: Semantic richness may protect against induced fixation: strong set induction hurt remote-associates performance only when the target had a narrow semantic network. The interaction is modest.
numbers: N=30 Chinese undergraduates, 2x2 within. Accessibility main effect F(1,29)=24.86, p<.001, eta2p=.46 (M=1.98 vs 0.98 correct). Induction x accessibility F(1,29)=4.88, p=.035, eta2p=.14. Low accessibility: weak induction 1.27 vs strong 0.70, p=.009, d=0.52; high accessibility: 1.90 vs 2.07, p=.538, d=0.12.
limits: The interaction p=.035 is borderline at N=30; single paradigm (Chinese remote associates); published 2026, not yet replicated.
agent_relevance: A candidate mechanism: fixation costs more when competing representations are hard to reach. Prompts that widen the candidate set may protect. Unproven.

source: Fang et al. (2026) Semantic accessibility is associated with reduced experience-induced heuristic fixation in creative problem solving
finding: The authors' own check with item-matched controls was only directional. The direct test that fixation cost was smaller under high accessibility did not reach significance.
numbers: 15 matched participant pairs. Low accessibility: induction cost weak M=0.122, d=0.893, p=.004; strong M=0.072, d=0.730, p=.013. High accessibility: weak M=0.072, p=.103, d=0.451; strong M=0.067, p=.104, d=0.449. Between-condition comparison of cost: strong t(14)=-0.133, p=.896; weak t(14)=-0.951, p=.358.
limits: The authors blame low power. For strong induction the high-accessibility cost (0.067) is about the same as the low-accessibility cost (0.072). Treat the buffer claim as unproven.
agent_relevance: Evidence for 'knowledge buffers fixation' is weak. Do not build a rule on it.

source: Huang, Tang and Hu (2018) Unconditional perseveration of the short-term mental set in chunk decomposition
finding: A short-term set built inside a session (5-8 practice problems versus one) blocks the unfamiliar solution on a later problem, even when the practice made the situation look similar to the test.
numbers: Exp 1, N=32. Accuracy: condition F(1,31)=6.58, p=.015, eta2=.18; solution x condition F(1,31)=11.00, p=.002, eta2=.26. The tight (unfamiliar) solution was correct less often after the enhanced set (t(31)=9.42, p=.004); the loose (familiar) solution was unaffected. Response time interaction F(1,31)=5.67, p=.024. Every participant chose the loose solution first.
limits: Chinese character chunk decomposition, one lab. Exact percentages are in figures not read.
agent_relevance: A short-term set forms in a few trials and needs no old habit. This matches the risk from a handful of same-method examples in context.

source: Huang, Tang and Hu (2018) Unconditional perseveration of the short-term mental set in chunk decomposition
finding: Boundary condition: when the test problem looks different and has only the unfamiliar solution, the set costs time and not accuracy. Similarity is not needed for the set to persist.
numbers: Exp 2, N=28. Accuracy: condition F(1,27)=0.02, p=.89; interaction F(1,27)=0.06, p=.81. Response time: condition F(1,27)=16.12, p<.001, eta2=.37; interaction F(1,27)=29.50, p<.001, eta2=.52. Time on the tight solution longer after the enhanced set, t(27)=23.85, p<.001.
limits: When no alternative route exists the set shows as delay. Measure time as well as accuracy.
agent_relevance: Include latency or token count as an outcome in any fixation test.

source: Gauselmann and Tempel (2025) Preventing fixation: item-method directed forgetting protecting against mental impasses in creative problem-solving
finding: Fixation from misleading primes disappeared when the prime words had been followed by a forget cue. Remember-cued primes cut performance by about 16 points.
numbers: N=72 (Prolific, German speakers), one outlier removed. Remember group (fixation-R): target items 27.3% vs control items 43.5%, t(35)=-5.53, p<.001, d=-0.92. Forget group (fixation-F): 36.7% vs 37.6%, t(34)=-0.33, p=.744, d=-0.06. Target items, R vs F: t(69)=-2.17, p=.033, d=-0.52.
limits: Brief report. The between-group difference on target items is modest (p=.033). Compound remote associates only, 2 target problems per person. Primes were words, not strategies.
agent_relevance: A concrete intervention that weakens the misleading item. An agent analogue: drop or demote the failed route from context before retrying. Untested for LLMs.

source: Gauselmann and Tempel (2025) Preventing fixation: item-method directed forgetting protecting against mental impasses in creative problem-solving
finding: The forgetting worked but not fully: forget-cued words were still recalled about a fifth of the time. Memory strength predicted how fixated a person was.
numbers: Final recall: remember items 46.6% vs forget items 19.8%, F(1,69)=89.21, p<.001, partial eta2=.56. Fixation words in the fixation-F group 15.7% vs neutral 45.0%, d=-1.43. Across people, recall of fixation words correlated with fixation size (control minus target solved), r=.35, p=.003.
limits: The correlation is exploratory. Recall of the prime is only a proxy for its activation during solving.
agent_relevance: Supports the inhibition account: the stronger the wrong route's activation, the larger the block. Suggests lowering the salience of failed attempts.

source: Beda and Smith (2018) Chasing red herrings: memory of distractors causes fixation in creative problem solving
finding: Strengthening memory of the wrong answer by repetition increased fixation, but the effect was small.
numbers: Exp 1, N=133 undergraduates. Two retrieval practices of red herrings vs zero: F(1,132)=5.167, p=.025, partial eta2=.038. Proportion solved: .44 (reinstated context, 0 practice), .38 (reinstated, 2), .42 (new context, 0), .41 (new context, 2). Context main effect F(1,132)=3.029, p=.084.
limits: Small effect (partial eta2=.038). Context reinstatement alone did not reach significance in Exp 1.
agent_relevance: More rehearsal of a wrong route means more block. Repeating a failed attempt in context may do harm.

source: Beda and Smith (2018) Chasing red herrings: memory of distractors causes fixation in creative problem solving
finding: Second experiment: fixation appeared only when the red herring's study context was reinstated at test. This is a retrieval-cue effect.
numbers: Exp 2, N=89. Unprimed M=.539 (SD .195); primed + reinstated context M=.456, t(88)=4.011, p<.001, d=.425 (about 8 points lower); primed + new context M=.506, vs unprimed t(88)=1.517, p=.399, d=.161. Reinstated vs new t(88)=2.585, p=.034, d=.274. Red-herring recall rose from .22 to .58 across two practices (d=1.66).
limits: Medium-small effect. Fixation was induced by a memory task, not by solving earlier problems.
agent_relevance: Fixation depends on whether cues in the problem match where the wrong answer was learned. A fresh framing may reduce retrieval of the stale route.

source: Kurtz et al. (2025) Relational encoding promotes creative insight for problem-solving
finding: A short pre-task that asks people to name relations between problem elements about doubled insight solving in Exp 1. Not an Einstellung test, but an intervention against an insight impasse.
numbers: Exp 1, N=136 after exclusions (168 recruited; 11 joke or blank answers, 4 experimenter error, 17 knew the two-string problem). Solved 22% (15/68) baseline vs 43% (29/68) relational encoding. Two-string problem chi2(1,67)=4.23, p=.039; peanut problem chi2(1,69)=2.57, p=.109.
limits: Two problems; the per-problem test was significant for one only. Heavy exclusions.
agent_relevance: A cheap process prompt: list relations between objects before solving. Candidate arm for an agent test.

source: Recover or discover: how outcome feedback shapes response patterns within game spaces (2026, npj Science of Learning)
finding: Old response patterns are easier to relearn than new ones; success keeps the old pattern and failure frees learning of a new one. Three experiments.
numbers: n=218 across three experiments. Mean Pre win rate 64.93%. Exp 1 (fixed 50% win rate in the middle phase): relearn old 66.16% vs learn new 61.39%, t(75)=3.25, p=.002. Exp 2 reinforcement (75%): old .694 vs new .592. Exp 3 (88%): old .725 vs new .622. Under 25% (punishment) the old-pattern advantage disappeared.
limits: Number-selection game against scripted opponents, not problem solving. Effects are 3 to 10 points.
agent_relevance: A model rewarded for a method may be more rigid than one that fails. Checks that confirm success can lock in a method; a failing check unlocks it.

source: Recover or discover: how outcome feedback shapes response patterns within game spaces (2026, npj Science of Learning)
finding: Stronger suppression of the earlier pattern in the middle phase predicted better learning of a new pattern later, whatever the feedback.
numbers: From the abstract and discussion: in most conditions retaining the old pattern beat acquiring new information; new learning never had an advantage over old.
limits: Correlational individual differences. The statistics for this predictor were not read in detail.
agent_relevance: Active suppression of the old route is the useful skill, not only exploring the new one.

source: Sheridan and Reingold (2013) The mechanisms and boundary conditions of the Einstellung effect in chess: evidence from eye movements
finding: Method details that bound the chess result: 17 experts and 17 novices; move quality was rated by human experts and by two engines.
numbers: 34 players (17 experts, mean CFC rating 2223, range 1876-2580; 17 unrated club novices). Move quality rated by five expert raters (some above 2300; two Grandmasters above 2500) and two engines (Houdini 2 Pro, Deep Rybka 4, about 3000 Elo). The 3-minute limit was reached on 10% of novice trials and 0% of expert trials.
limits: Experts here were mostly Experts and Candidate Masters, below the masters in Bilalic et al. 2008. Four problems only.
agent_relevance: Engine plus panel scoring is an external check of 'better move', like a verifier for an agent.

source: Sheridan and Reingold (2013) The mechanisms and boundary conditions of the Einstellung effect in chess: evidence from eye movements
finding: The paper states that Bilalic et al. found the effect across Candidate Masters, Masters and International Masters, which is the claim this paper tests at a lower rating.
numbers: Introduction only: the earlier study covered Candidate Master to International Master range. No new numbers here.
limits: Secondary statement of prior work inside this paper. Primary numbers are in the A10.01 file.
agent_relevance: Link to A10.01 and E16.01 for chess numbers.

source: Explaining success in Bayesian reasoning with the adaptive toolbox and expertise (2026, Psychonomic Bulletin and Review)
finding: Review of Bayesian-reasoning training: some learners given natural frequencies converted them back to probabilities, and prior familiarity with formula methods shaped which training worked.
numbers: Cites Weber et al. 2018 (quote about an Einstellung toward probabilities) and Kim et al. 2024 (those already familiar with formulas gained little or equal from frequencies). No sample sizes given.
limits: Secondary review; the primary studies were not opened.
agent_relevance: Prior method familiarity can reduce gain from a better representation. Test: offer a better representation to a model already prompted with the old method.

source: Fang et al. (2026) Semantic accessibility is associated with reduced experience-induced heuristic fixation in creative problem solving
finding: Introduction cites neural evidence that repeated use of one strategy lowers early dorsal anterior cingulate (dACC) activity, i.e. conflict detection weakens as the set grows.
numbers: Citation to Huang et al. 2019; no numbers given in this article.
limits: Secondary mention; the primary study was not opened.
agent_relevance: Supports a conflict-detection account of the set. Argues for an explicit 'is there a cheaper route' check.
